topic: Linear and binary search: tracing, invariants and test cases
scope: Original partial support for AQA GCSE Computer Science 8525, first teaching September 2025, sections 3.1.1-3 checked 2026-10-19. prerequisites: Read ordered lists and distinguish an index from a stored value.
Follow assignment, comparison, selection and repetition.
objectives: Trace linear and binary search with explicit indexing and stopping rules.
Explain why binary search needs ordered data.
Compare search methods using stated costs and assumptions.
Design boundary tests and identify off-by-one errors.

notes.heading: Specify the search contract before tracing
paragraphs: A search takes a collection and a target value and determines whether an appropriate match exists. Decide what the output means before following an algorithm. This lesson returns the zero-based index of one matching element, or −1 when no match exists. Index 0 is a valid first position, so it must not be confused with failure. With duplicate target values, returning any matching index is different from promising the first match; the ordinary binary search below promises only one match.

An algorithm is the method, while a program is one implementation of it. A trace records changing state for a particular input; it can illustrate behaviour without proving that every input works. Our lists permit direct access by index. Empty lists, missing targets and targets at either boundary are part of the contract, not optional inconveniences. In a written response, state the data, target, indexing convention and return convention so that the examiner or reviewer can reproduce the same trace.

notes.heading: Linear search checks candidates in sequence
paragraphs: Linear search begins at the first element and compares each candidate with the target until it finds a match or exhausts the list. In this lesson's editorial pseudocode: for i from 0 through length−1, return i if items[i] equals target; after the loop return −1. The failure return belongs after the loop, not after the first failed comparison. Otherwise the method would incorrectly give up whenever the first item was not the target.

The method does not require sorted input because it does not discard unexamined values based on order. When searching for a single value, finding a match allows an early return. In the worst case for n items, it inspects n candidates: this occurs for a missing target or a target first matched at the end. An empty list inspects no candidates. This count describes element inspections, not necessarily every machine instruction, and the exact elapsed time also depends on implementation and data access.

notes.heading: Binary search maintains a shrinking candidate interval
paragraphs: Binary search uses sorted ascending data and keeps inclusive bounds low and high around positions that might still contain the target. Initialise low=0 and high=length−1. While low≤high, choose mid=floor((low+high)/2). If items[mid] equals the target, return mid. If the middle value is smaller, set low=mid+1. If it is larger, set high=mid−1. When the bounds cross, return −1. These are editorial rules for this lesson, not a quotation of an official pseudocode language.

Ordering justifies eliminating a half: if the middle value is too small, all values at earlier indices are also too small for this ascending list. The useful invariant is that any remaining match, if one exists, lies inside the current interval. Each unsuccessful iteration excludes the already-tested midpoint and shrinks that interval. Keeping the midpoint by setting low=mid can prevent progress near the boundary. An empty list begins with high=−1, so the loop condition fails immediately without indexing an element.

notes.heading: Trace values, indices and comparisons separately
paragraphs: Use columns for low, high, mid, middle value and the decision. For the list [2,5,8,11,14,17,20] and target 17, the first midpoint is index 3 with value 11. The next interval is indices 4 through 6, whose midpoint is index 5 with value 17. The output is 5, not 17, because the contract returns an index. If a one-based position is requested instead, convert the output explicitly rather than changing conventions halfway through.

Define what a comparison count means. We count one middle-element inspection per binary-search iteration, even if an implementation performs an equality test followed by an order test on that element. For the example, two elements are inspected. A different midpoint convention can change the exact trace on even-length intervals, so state the floor rule used here. A missing-target trace must continue until low exceeds high; stopping when only one candidate remains would skip a valid final check. Keep the output separate from the number of inspections.

notes.heading: Choose an algorithm using the workload
paragraphs: Binary search often inspects far fewer elements than linear search in a large sorted, directly indexable list because it repeatedly reduces the candidate interval. That does not mean it is automatically the best choice for every task. An unsorted list must be prepared into a suitable order before ordinary binary search applies. For one search, preparation may cost more than simply scanning; for many searches over stable data, the preparation may be worthwhile. This lesson compares reasoning about time without requiring formal asymptotic notation.

Sorting can also change indices. If an application needs the original position of an item, reordering the values without preserving their original indices changes the meaning of the result. Frequent insertions or updates can create additional maintenance work. Strings require a consistent ordering rule; a human alphabetical assumption may differ from a program's comparator. State the relevant data and workload assumptions before concluding that one approach is more efficient. Neither an inspection count on one input nor a single timed run establishes universal superiority.

notes.heading: Test boundary behaviour and explain defects
paragraphs: A small test suite should include an empty list, a one-item match, a one-item miss, first and last matches, an internal match, a missing value between present values, and a value outside the list's range. For duplicate values, check the promised contract: any valid matching index is acceptable here, while a first-occurrence search would need extra logic. Test lists must meet the algorithm's preconditions; an unsorted binary-search test can demonstrate misuse, not necessarily a defect in the specified algorithm.

When a trace fails, identify the first state that violates the intended rule. Returning failure inside a linear-search loop discards unchecked items. Keeping a failed midpoint can make a binary interval stop shrinking. Using length rather than length−1 as an inclusive high bound can access outside the list. Explain the consequence and the correction, then replay a boundary case. These exercises support searching mechanics and trace reasoning, but sorting methods, full flowchart construction, broad decomposition and executable-language practice remain separate work in the mapped course.

notes.heading: Specifying which duplicate a search must return
paragraphs: Finding any matching value is a different contract from finding the first matching index. An ordinary binary search can stop when it encounters equality, which may return a middle duplicate. To find the first match in a sorted ascending array, retain the equal index as a candidate and continue searching to its left. If no earlier equal value is found, return the retained candidate. The invariant now includes both the remaining candidate interval and the best equal index seen so far. Make indexing and midpoint rounding explicit when tracing. An empty array and an absent target still need defined results; this example uses -1 for absence.

workedExamples.prompt: Binary-search [2,5,8,11,14,17,20] for 17 with floor midpoint and inclusive bounds.
steps: low=0, high=6, mid=3; 11 is too small, so low=4.
mid=2 gives 8, so high=1; the bounds cross.

workedExamples.prompt: What happens for an empty list?
steps: Linear search has no indices to visit.
Binary search starts low=0, high=−1, so its loop is not entered.
workedExamples.answer: Both return −1 with zero element inspections.

workedExamples.prompt: Why can low=mid cause a loop for [3,7] searching for 7?
steps: low=0, high=1 gives mid=0 and value 3.
Updating low to mid leaves low=0 and repeats the same state.
workedExamples.answer: The incorrect update may never shrink the interval.

workedExamples.prompt: Trace first-match binary search for target 4 in zero-indexed [1, 4, 4, 4, 9]. Use inclusive low/high bounds, floor midpoint, candidate initially -1, and on equality store mid then set high = mid - 1.
steps: At low 0, high 4, mid 2 matches: candidate 2, high 1.
At low 0, high 1, mid 0 contains 1, so set low 1.
At low 1, high 1, mid 1 matches: candidate 1, high 0; the interval is empty and return 1.
workedExamples.answer: Midpoint indices are 2, 0, 1; the returned first matching index is 1.

misconceptions.claim: Binary search works on any list because it tests the middle.
misconceptions.correction: Discarding halves requires the stated ordering precondition.
Index 0 is the first element; this contract uses −1 for failure.

misconceptions.claim: A single successful trace proves an algorithm correct.
misconceptions.correction: It demonstrates that case; boundary tests and reasoning are also needed.

questions.prompt: Which condition justifies discarding a half in this binary-search algorithm?
options: The target must be the first value.
The list is sorted ascending under the same comparison rule.
The list must contain an even number of values.
questions.answer: The list is sorted ascending under the same comparison rule.
solution: The midpoint comparison must imply something about other values.
Ascending order supplies that implication.

questions.prompt: Linear-search [7,2,9,4,12] for 4. How many elements are inspected before returning?
questions.answer: 4 inspections.
solution: Inspect 7, then 2, then 9.
The fourth inspected value is the match 4.
markingPoints: State four inspections, not index three.

questions.prompt: Binary-search [1,4,7,10,13,16,19] for 16 using the lesson's rules. Give the midpoint indices visited and returned index.
questions.answer: Visited 3 then 5; returned index 5.
solution: The first midpoint value is 10, so restrict to indices 4 through 6.
The next midpoint is index 5 with value 16.

questions.prompt: For [1,4,7,10,13,16,19] and target 12, how many middle-element inspections does binary search make using inclusive bounds and floor midpoint?
questions.answer: 3 inspections.
solution: Index 3 has 10, so low becomes 4.
Index 5 has 16, so high becomes 4.
Index 4 has 13, so high becomes 3 and the loop ends.

questions.prompt: Explain why updating low to mid rather than mid+1 can fail in an inclusive-bound binary search.
questions.answer: The already-tested midpoint may remain in the interval. In a two-item interval the floor midpoint can equal low, so low=mid makes no progress and repeats the state.
solution: Identify the excluded candidate that should be removed.
Use the two-item boundary case.
Give the progress-preserving update.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum number of element inspections for a linear search over 12 items under this contract?
solution: A missing target forces examination of every item.
There are 12 candidates.

questions.prompt: What does returned index 0 mean under this lesson's contract?
options: A match at the first element.
The target value must be zero.
questions.answer: A match at the first element.
solution: Indices start at zero.
Failure is represented by −1 instead.

questions.prompt: What should binary search return for an empty list, and why is no element access needed?
questions.answer: −1; low=0 and high=−1 make the loop condition false immediately.
solution: Calculate the initial bounds.
Apply low≤high before reading an item.

questions.prompt: An application needs one lookup in an unsorted list and must report the original index. Why is 'binary search is always faster' inadequate?
questions.answer: Sorting has a time cost and changes positions unless original indices are retained. For one lookup, a linear scan may be more suitable; the workload and indexing contract matter.
solution: Identify required preparation.
Identify output-meaning risk.
Qualify the efficiency comparison.

questions.prompt: A search implementation returns −1 after the first nonmatching element. Give a failing test and explain the correction.
questions.answer: Searching [3,8] for 8 fails incorrectly after 3. Keep checking later elements and return −1 only after the loop has exhausted every candidate.
solution: Choose a target beyond the first position.
Trace the premature failure.
Move the failure return outside the loop.

questions.prompt: Trace first-match binary search for target 4 in zero-indexed [1, 4, 4, 4, 9]. Use inclusive low/high bounds, floor midpoint, candidate initially -1, and on equality store mid then set high = mid - 1.
questions.answer: Midpoint indices are 2, 0, 1; the returned first matching index is 1.
solution: At low 0, high 4, mid 2 matches: candidate 2, high 1.
At low 0, high 1, mid 0 contains 1, so set low 1.
At low 1, high 1, mid 1 matches: candidate 1, high 0; the interval is empty and return 1.
markingPoints: At low 0, high 4, mid 2 matches: candidate 2, high 1.
At low 0, high 1, mid 0 contains 1, so set low 1.

questions.prompt: A learner stops at midpoint 2 and reports that first-match search succeeded. Explain which contract it satisfies and what must change for the requested contract.
questions.answer: Index 2 satisfies any-match search but not first-match search. Retain it and continue left on equality to seek an earlier match.
solution: The value at index 2 equals the target.
Index 1 also contains 4 and is earlier.
Continuing in the left interval after equality distinguishes first-match from any-match behaviour.
markingPoints: The value at index 2 equals the target.
Index 1 also contains 4 and is earlier.
Continuing in the left interval after equality distinguishes first-match from any-match behaviour.
